draws.answer: That is African swine fever. Confine your goats and stop any movement of animals on or off the place. Keep all outside visitors away from the pen. history.content: I see a purple pink flowered weed clinging around the base of my sorghum plants that are stunted. What should I do?

After the sorghum is up and reaching its panicle stage, plant a legume such as cowpea or soybean in the same field to fix the nitrogen. For a reliable method of controlling Striga, visit ICAT.

history.content: is the purple weed just a nutrient deficiency problem

draws.answer: It is not a nutrient deficiency, it is a group of plants caused by the parasitic weed Striga. To control Striga, pull it out before it flowers and cut the stems of any plants that are heavily infested. Then sow your maize on patches where the strong roots of striga-free zones are present. Rotate the plot with a striga-tolerant maize variety. For advice on resistant varieties or whether a fungicide is needed, go to ICAT.

It is not a nutrient deficiency, it is a parasitic weed that makes the maize look yellow because it consumes the nitrogen in the roots. Look-alike is nitrogen shortage, which shows as a uniform pale yellowing of the older leaves while the new ones stay greener, without any spots or streaks. The weed you see is groundnut leaf spot, a fungal problem that shows rounder darker lesions. Because it is a parasite, you must act immediately: plant a tolerant variety, clear or bury all old groundnut residues, rotate with cereals and do not grow groundnut on the same land year after year. Get help with resistant varieties from ICAT and rotate from cereals to a legume.

history.content: What is the recommended management for Striga hermonthica on sorghum?

draws.answer: The recommendation is to avoid planting sorghum on the same plot in consecutive years; instead, rotate with a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean. When the sorghum is at panicle initiation, about 30-35 days after sowing, use 10-15 kg per hectare of striga tolerance seed. Weed early, with the first weeding about 2 weeks after sowing. After harvest, clear or bury all sorghum residues to stop the fungus from carrying over. For the variety that matches your region and season, go to ICAT.

The recommendation is to avoid growing sorghum on the same plot for more than two consecutive years, which reduces the parasite pressure. Also sow a cereal after the sorghum harvest so the cereal can use the nitrogen left by the sorghum root nodules. Do not grow sorghum after maize because the maize is often taken up by the same parasites. Use early-array seed with a fungicide-insecticide coating if needed. For a soil-specific advice on whether to apply 25 to 35 kg per hectare of NPK or a specific fungicide, visit ICAT.

history.content: My herd has sudden diarrhoea and many goats are dying quickly, almost all of them. What is happening?

draws.answer: The problem is leucaena poisoning in your cattle. First cut leucaena back so it is only a quarter to a third of the total ration and never the main feed. Then mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to give the rumen plenty of roughage. Change the feed gradually over several days, keeping clean water and a mineral or salt source always available. If the appetite does not recover or you see drooling, a swollen throat, or bloat, call the veterinary service.

history.content: What steps should I take against Striga hermonthica on my sorghum?

draws.answer: Striga hermonthica is the weed that competes with sorghum for nutrients and water. Plant a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the same field and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Before sowing sorghum, sow a legume at the right time and make sure the soil is rich and well-drained. After sorghum, always plant a nitrogen-fixing legume and cut the legume stems at ground level. For help choosing the legume or checking soil fertility, go to ICAT.
